opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a big question, and I'll share how I see it, though nobody really knows the exact path yet.

For a long time robotics progressed one task at a time. You wanted a robot to pick up a cup, so you built a perception pipeline, a grasp planner, and a controller, and tuned everything for that cup on that table. It worked, but it didn't transfer. Each new task was basically a new research project. That's the opposite of general.

What's changed in the last few years is that we've started borrowing the recipe that worked for language and vision: large models trained on lots of diverse data, which then show surprising generalization. Vision-language-action models are an example. You take a model that already understands the world from internet-scale text and images, and you teach it to output actions. Suddenly the robot can follow instructions it was never explicitly trained on, recognize objects it has never touched, and do some reasoning about what the person actually wants. That was a big conceptual shift for the field.

But I don't think simply scaling that recipe gets us all the way, for a few reasons.

The first is data. Language models had the whole internet. Robotics has no equivalent. Robot data is expensive: you need physical hardware, people to teleoperate, and time, and every hour of data is still just one hour. So a central question is how to get orders of magnitude more useful data. I think the answer is a combination: teleoperation at larger scale, simulation, learning from human videos, and eventually robots collecting their own data through deployment and self-improvement. Simulation is something I've worked on a lot, and I still believe in it, especially for locomotion and dynamic skills, but the sim-to-real gap for contact-rich manipulation, like deformable objects or liquids, is still hard.

The second is embodiment. A language model has one interface, text. Robots come in very different bodies: arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, different hands and sensors. A truly general robot brain has to transfer across embodiments, or at least adapt to a new one quickly. We're seeing early signs that cross-embodiment training helps, which is encouraging, but it's far from solved.

The third is the gap between high-level understanding and low-level physical skill. Today's models are surprisingly good at the "what": understanding the scene, planning the steps. They're still much weaker at the "how": dexterity, force control, recovering when something slips. Humans take this for granted. Folding laundry or tying a shoelace seems trivial to us, but it's extremely hard for robots. This is the old Moravec's paradox, and it's still very real.

So my picture of the path forward is something like this. First, foundation models give robots common sense and semantic generalization, which is now largely there in early form. Second, we scale physical data and improve the learning algorithms so low-level dexterity becomes more general, and I think this is where most of the hard work is right now. Third, robots go out into the real world, at first in constrained settings, and the deployment itself creates a data flywheel. The robots that are useful get deployed more, collect more data, and become more capable. That flywheel is what made other AI fields take off, and robotics doesn't have it yet at scale.

And one thing I'd add is that safety and reliability matter much more for robots than for chatbots. If a language model makes a mistake, you get a wrong sentence. If a robot makes a mistake, it can break something or hurt someone. So "general" has to come with "reliable," and that will probably slow down how fast these systems reach homes, compared with how fast the research demos improve.

So I'm optimistic. I think we're at an inflection point, and the progress in the last two or three years is the fastest I've seen in my career. But I'd say we're at the beginning of the curve, not near the end. The general-purpose robot that walks into your home and just helps with whatever you need is coming, but there's still a lot of fundamental research between here and there.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that we're at a moment that looks a lot like where language models were around 2019 or 2020. The ingredients are visible, but the recipe hasn't fully come together yet.

Let me break down how I see the path. In the past, robotics progressed task by task. You'd spend a year getting a robot to open a door, then another year on grasping, and nothing transferred. What has changed is that we now have a working hypothesis for how to escape that: treat robot behavior as another modality that a large pretrained model can learn, and scale it with data the same way we scaled language and vision. Foundation models already give us a surprising amount of common sense about the physical world for free. A model can look at a kitchen and tell you what a mug is, what it's for, and roughly how to pick it up. That semantic understanding used to be the hard part, and now it's essentially a solved problem we inherit.

The bottleneck has shifted to the low-level control side, and to data. Language had the internet. Robotics has no equivalent, because every demonstration costs real time on real hardware. So I think the next few years are going to be defined by three parallel efforts. First, scaling real-world teleoperation data across many robot embodiments, so models learn skills that transfer across bodies rather than being tied to one specific arm. Second, simulation, which is where a lot of my own work has been. Sim gives you essentially unlimited data for locomotion and contact-rich tasks, and the sim-to-real gap has narrowed enough that policies trained entirely in simulation now walk on real legged robots in environments they've never seen. Third, and this is the one I'm most excited about, is using the models themselves to generate the training signal. A language model can write reward functions, propose tasks, critique failures, and essentially act as a tireless teacher. That closes the loop in a way that could compound.

Where I'd push back on the hype is the word "truly general." I don't think we'll wake up one day with a robot that can do everything. It'll come in layers. Locomotion is nearly there. Simple pick-and-place in structured environments is close. Dexterous manipulation of deformable objects, working safely around people, recovering gracefully from the thousand small things that go wrong in a real home, those are still years out and will require advances in hardware, not just algorithms. Hands in particular are a real constraint. And safety matters more here than in software, because a bad action has physical consequences, so the reliability bar is much higher than it is for a chatbot.

So my view is that we'll see steady, visible progress rather than a single breakthrough. The flywheel of better models producing more capable robots, which collect more data, which train better models, has just started spinning. Once it gets going, I think the pace will surprise people, the same way language models did.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to build robots that can learn many different skills and reuse what they’ve learned in new situations. Today, we can make a robot very good at a particular task, but if you change the environment or ask it to do something slightly different, it can struggle. General capability means being able to adapt without having an engineer redesign the system each time.

One major challenge is data. A language model can learn from enormous amounts of text, but a robot needs experience interacting with the physical world. That experience is much harder to collect. I think we’ll need a combination of real-world robot data, simulation, and knowledge learned from images, videos, and language. Simulation lets us practice at scale, while real-world experience tells us where our assumptions break down.

We also need to connect high-level understanding with reliable physical skills. Knowing that you should pick up a cup is different from knowing how to grasp it without slipping or breaking it. A general robot needs both—and it needs to recognize a mistake and recover.

So I expect progress to be gradual: systems that handle more tasks, in more environments, with less supervision. The important milestone is when learning one task makes the next task easier. That’s when we start moving beyond a collection of specialized skills toward something more general.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the path to general robotics is to build systems that can learn many skills and reuse them in new situations. Today, we can make a robot do a particular task very well, but changing the environment or the task often requires a lot of additional engineering. The next step is to make that adaptation part of the robot’s learning process.

That requires progress on several fronts. We need models that connect perception, reasoning, and physical action. We need much more diverse experience, both from real robots and from simulation. And we need ways for robots to learn from failures safely, because interacting with the physical world is very different from generating an answer on a computer.

I expect progress to be gradual. We’ll see robots become useful across a broader range of tasks in constrained environments, and then expand from there. The real test of generality is whether a robot can handle a situation its designers didn’t anticipate, using skills it already has.
